When a sentence has both an indirect pronoun (to whom?) and a direct one (whom? / what?), the indirect comes FIRST and its i becomes E: mi → me, ti → te, ci → ce, vi → ve.
Just like Romanian "mi-l", "ți-o": the indirect comes first. The difference: Italian writes them separately (me lo), but in the 3rd person joins everything into one word (glielo).
2. Glielo: for him, her, them and the polite you
In the 3rd person, gli and le both become GLIE- and join lo / la / li / le / ne. So "glielo" can mean "it to him", "to her" or "to them" — context tells you:
The present? I'll give it to him tomorrow. (to Pietro)
The letter? I'll write it to her myself. (to Giulia)
The tickets? I'll send them to them tonight. (to the parents)
Not "le lo" for her! Always "glielo": "Lo dico a Giulia" → "Glielo dico".
3. Double pronouns in the passato prossimo
Lo / la become l' before AVERE, and the participle agrees with the DIRECT pronoun:
Who gave it to you (the watch)?
Matei gave it to me (the scarf).
They sent them to us (the flowers).
I talked to him / her about it.
Devo dirtelo. / Te lo devo dire.
With the short imperatives da', di', fa', sta', va' the pronoun's consonant doubles: dammelo, dimmelo, fammelo vedere. But not with gli: "Diglielo!".

On the 12th of July Pietro woke up at six. That had never happened before. He ran into the kitchen, but his grandmother was pretending nothing was going on: she was making coffee and listening to the radio, as she did every morning.

"Grandma, do you know what day it is today?" "Saturday," Graziella answered without turning round. "But it's the 12th of July!" "Oh, really? So what?" Pietro went back to his room, offended. He was thinking: "They've all forgotten."

At ten someone rang the bell. Pietro didn't want to open the door. "You go, Grandma." "My hands are in the flour. You go." Pietro opened the door reluctantly… and found her right in front of him: his mum, with a bunch of balloons, and his dad, with an enormous parcel.

For a second he said nothing. Then he shouted so loudly that Michelangelo ran off onto the roof. "Why didn't you tell me?" "Because it was a surprise," said Sara, hugging him. "Grandma managed it: she didn't tell you for two weeks. A record."

The party was in the trattoria, in the afternoon. Everyone was there: his schoolmates, Signor Franco, even Professor Bellini, who brought a book about the stars ("For a future astronaut," he said. Someone had told him.)
Matei and Giulia arrived last. Giulia was holding the parcel with the red ribbon. "This one is from someone who keeps his promises," she said.

Pietro opened it in three seconds. Inside were the blue watch and a card: "For Pietro, who's always late for school, but always on time for ice cream. I promised it to you. Now you have no more excuses. Matei." Pietro put it on his wrist straight away and never took it off again, not even to sleep.
Then came Graziella's cake: chocolate and strawberries, with nine candles. "Make a wish!" his mum told him. Pietro closed his eyes, thought hard and blew out all the candles in one breath.

"What did you wish for?" Giulia asked him. "I can't tell you. If I tell you, it won't come true." But later, when everyone was leaving, Pietro took Matei by the hand and said quietly: "I'll tell you, because you're a man. I wished that Mum and Dad would come back to live in Florence."

Matei didn't answer. But across the room he saw Marco and Sara talking to Graziella in low voices, serious, and Graziella wiping her eyes with her apron. Maybe someone had already heard that wish, even before the candles.
